say: Welcome back, inquirers! Look around any shop in Singapore and you will see percentages everywhere: 20% off, 9% GST, prices up 10%. Shops are very good at percentages. Today we make sure we are better.
Notice it, test it, explain why. Today the big question is always: percentage of WHAT?
Here are three hundred-squares. Each one has 100 small squares. Write how much is shaded as a percentage, and how much is NOT shaded. Whiteboards up when I say go.
Did anyone find the "not shaded" part without counting? How?
A bicycle costs $200. The price goes up by 10%. Later the new price goes down by 10%. What is the price now? Write your prediction before you work anything out.
Thumbs up if you think it is back to $200. Thumbs down if you think it is less. Sideways if you think it is more.
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: what is 10% of $200? Add it on. Now what is 10% of the NEW price?
Got $200: check which amount you took 10% of the second time. Was it $200 or $220?
If a pair wants more: try up 50% then down 50%. Is the gap bigger or smaller than with 10%?

say: “I want 45% of $60. 10% is one tenth, so I divide by 10: $6. Half of that is 5%: $3. 45% is four 10%s and one 5%: $24 + $3 = $27.”
“98% is nearly all of it. So I find what is missing: 2%. 1% of $60 is 60 cents, so 2% is $1.20, and 98% is $60 − $1.20 = $58.80.”
“For the fan I take off the discount first: 15% of $120 is $18, so the sale price is $102. The GST is 9% of $102, not of $120. 10% of $102 is $10.20, 1% is $1.02, so 9% is $9.18. I pay $111.18.”

do: Ask: “Percentage of what? Point to the whole.”
Ask: “Can you build that percentage from 10%, 5% and 1%?”
Ask: “After the first change, what is the new whole?”
stuck: Hint 2: “Draw a bar for the whole and cut it into 10 equal parts.”
Hint 3: “Write what the whole is BEFORE you work out each percentage.”

do: Ask: “Percentage of what? Point to the whole.”
Ask: “Can you build that percentage from 10%, 5% and 1%?”
Ask: “After the first change, what is the new whole?”
stuck: Hint 2: “Draw a bar for the whole and cut it into 10 equal parts.”
Hint 3: “Write what the whole is BEFORE you work out each percentage.”

say: “Which is better for the shopper: add 9% GST first and then take 20% off, or take 20% off first and then add 9% GST?”
“Mei says 20% off and then 9% GST is the same as 11% off. Is she right?”
ask: “Which is better for the shopper: add 9% GST first and then take 20% off, or take 20% off first and then add 9% GST?”

They give exactly the same price. On $100: GST first gives $109, then 20% off gives $87.20; 20% off first gives $80, then GST gives $87.20. Each change multiplies the price, and the order of multiplying does not matter. Mei is not right: 11% off $100 is $89, not $87.20, because the 9% GST is worked out on the smaller sale price.

say: “Today you found that percentages can trick you when the whole changes. Before every percentage, ask: of what? Well done, inquirers!”
“Show me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p5l7-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Find any percentage of an amount by building it from 10%, 5% and 1%; work out a discount and then 9% GST on the sale price; find a percentage of a remainder; spot the classic percentage traps. A puzzle that goes further (Think harder page only): find a percentage increase or decrease by comparing the change with the ORIGINAL amount. Thinking strategies taught today: ASK "PERCENTAGE OF WHAT?", BUILD FROM 10%, 5% AND 1%, and DRAW A BAR MODEL. GST in Singapore is 9%. Materials: mini whiteboard and marker, workbook, pencil, a hundred-square page or squared paper. A calculator only for checking at the end of each page. Online: children keep the workbook and a whiteboard in front of the camera. The tutor screen-shares the slides and draws bar models with the annotation tool. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5 (one hold-up for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6.5 to 12 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 12 to 24.5 (pair work 6 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 24.5 to 35.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 35.5 to 40, workbook page 1 40 to 54 (the questions without a star; after question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 54 to 57.5, short teaching before page 2 57.5 to 59, workbook page 2 59 to 70.5 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 70.5 to 73.5, talk time 73.5 to 79 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 79 to 84.5, reflection 84.5 to 87 (pass is always OK), stamp typed in the chat and goodbye 87 to 88, and the buffer 88 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation."

p5l7-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE hold-up for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone shows their paper at the same moment (own paper shown only to you as you walk round; online, all hold paper to the camera together, or show it to you only, on camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: 65 squares, which is 65%. Percent means out of 100.; Q2: No. $100 → $90 → $81. 20% off $100 would be $80. The second 10% is taken from $90, not from $100. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4.5 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: everyone holds their paper up to the camera at the same moment, or shows it to you only, on camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE hold-up for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone shows their paper at the same moment), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l7-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 9. Hundred-Square Snap. Show the three squares one at a time (cover the other two with your hand or paper online). Children write on whiteboards: the percentage shaded and the percentage NOT shaded, then hold them up together. Click to show the answers. Square 1: 30 shaded (3 full rows) so 30% shaded, 70% not shaded. Square 2: 45 shaded (4 rows and 5 more) so 45% and 55%. Square 3: 64 shaded (6 rows and 4 more) so 64% and 36%. Ask: "Who found the not-shaded part without counting? How?" (100 take away the shaded part.) "Why is the whole 100?" (percent means out of 100). Listen for: children counting every small square. Praise rows of 10: each row is 10%.

p5l7-warm2.note: Minutes 9 to 12. Read each aloud, whiteboards up together, then click to show. Ask "How did you do it?" each time. 1) 50% is half: $45. 2) 10% is one tenth: 350 ÷ 10 = 35. 3) 25% is a quarter: 48 ÷ 4 = 12. 4) 1% is one hundredth: $700 ÷ 100 = $7. Answers: $45, 35, 12, $7. If you are short of time, skip question 4.

p5l7-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 24.5 (the whole explore; this slide 12 to 20.5). Pairs predict first (thumbs: back to $200, less, or more?) and write the prediction. Then they work it out on whiteboards. Most children predict $200. Let them find out for themselves. Pair work is at most 6 minutes. Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): try up 50% then down 50% on $80. Is the gap bigger or smaller than with 10%? PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 6 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 20.5 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: Up 50% then down 50%: $200 → $300 → $150. Up 20% then down 20%: $200 → $240 → $192. The final price is always LESS than $200, because the "down" percentage is taken from the bigger new price.

p5l7-explore2.note: Minutes 20.5 to 24.5. Pencils down: gather the pairs, then draw both routes on the board. Answers: 1) No. $200, up 10% is $220 (10% of $200 = $20). Down 10% of $220 is $22 off, so $198. (Not asked together: does the order matter? No: down first gives $200 − $20 = $180, then up 10% is $18 more = $198. Same answer.) 2) The two 10%s are of different amounts: $20 added, but $22 taken off, because the second 10% is of the NEW price. That is why it is $2 less. Write on the board: "Percentage of WHAT?" This question is the heart of the lesson. After a change, the new price is the new whole. Do NOT teach the method for the worksheet yet: the next slides do that. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): Up 50% then down 50%: $200 → $300 → $150. Up 20% then down 20%: $200 → $240 → $192. The final price is always LESS than $200, because the "down" percentage is taken from the bigger new price.

p5l7-teach1.note: Minutes 24.5 to 26.5. Teach. Point to the bar: "100% is the whole thing. Cut it into 10 equal parts: each part is 10%." Then the three tools. Click to show each example with $80 (a different amount from the worksheet): 10% of $80 = $8; 5% is half of that, $4; 1% is $80 ÷ 100 = $0.80. Ask: "How can we make 15% from these?" (10% + 5% = $8 + $4 = $12.) "35%?" (3 × 10% + 5%.) Think-aloud: "I never learn a new rule for each percentage. I build it from 10%, 5% and 1%." Money check: 1% of $80 is 80 cents, so write $0.80, not $0.08.

p5l7-we1.note: Minutes 26.5 to 28.5. Click to reveal each step and let children say the step first. Think-aloud: "10% is one tenth: $6. 5% is half of 10%: $3. 45% is four 10%s and one 5%: four sixes are 24, add 3: $27." Then: "For 98% I could add lots of pieces, but 98% is only 2% away from the whole. I take the 2% off: 1% is 60 cents, so 2% is $1.20. $60 take away $1.20 is $58.80." Check: 45% + 55% should make $60: 55% of $60 is $33, and $27 + $33 = $60. Ask: "When is take-away the clever way?" (when the percentage is close to 100%).

p5l7-we2.note: Minutes 30 to 32. Click to reveal each step. Ask first: "What do we take the 9% of: $120 or $102?" (the price after the discount: that is what the shop charges for the fan). Step 1: 10% of $120 is $12, 5% is $6, so 15% is $18; $102 is the sale price. Step 2: 10% of $102 is $10.20; 1% is $1.02; 9% is 10% take away 1%: $9.18. Step 3: add. Think-aloud: "GST in Singapore is 9%. It is added to what you actually pay for the thing, so I work it out on the sale price." Check by estimating: 9% is a bit less than 10% of $102 = $10.20. $9.18 is a bit less. Sensible. The machine picture shows the chain: price, discount, sale price, GST, final price.

p5l7-try2.note: Minutes 32 to 34. Whiteboards. a) 25% is a quarter: $20 off, $60. b) 10% of $200 = $20, 1% = $2, so 9% = $18. Watch for children who work out GST on the old price instead of the sale price. (Two items only.)

p5l7-key.note: Minutes 34 to 35.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Adding percentages of different wholes: 20% of the money and then 25% of the REMAINDER is not 45% of the money. (2) Thinking that up 25% and then down 25% brings the price back to the start. (3) Working out a percentage increase or decrease using the new amount instead of the ORIGINAL amount, or working out GST on the price before the discount.

p5l7-break.note: Minutes 35.5 to 40. 4.5 minutes. Online: children show the position on camera. Let children call the next percentage. Ask: "What percentage is half way between 50% and 100%?" (75%: hands on shoulders). Then a drink of water.

p5l7-ws1.note: Minutes 40 to 54. Walk around. Ask "Percentage of what?" before giving any help. Q1: check the boxes you already have before working out 35%. Q2 (the rice cooker, the longest) is done in the page 2 time, so leave it for now. Q3c: do not accept "yes" without working out the final price. Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 3 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q1 (a) (b) and Q3 (a) (b) (c); Q2 is done in the page 2 time. Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l7-ws1ans.note: Minutes 54 to 57.5. One pair explains Q3 (page 1 in class is Q1 and Q3; Q2 is checked on the page 2 check slide). Click after a pair explains theirs. Q1: 35% = 3 × $24 + $12 = $84. 99% = $240 − $2.40 = $237.60. Q3: $80 + $20 = $100 after the 25% rise; 20% of $100 is $20, so back to $80. The second percentage is of the new whole.

p5l7-teachrem.note: Minutes 57.5 to 59. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 has a remainder). Draw the bar of $80 in 4 equal parts: each part is $20, which is 25%. Click 1: one part spent, $60 left, and that $60 is the NEW whole. Click 2: the 40% is of $60, not of $80. 10% of $60 is $6, so 40% is $24. $36 is left. Click 3: the trap. 25% + 40% = 65% suggests 35% is left, which would be $28. Wrong. The real fraction left is $36 out of $80: 36 ÷ 80 = 0.45, so 45%. Ask: "Why can we not add 25% and 40%?" (they are percentages of different wholes: $80 and $60). Check: spent $20 + $24 = $44, which is 55% of $80, and 55% + 45% = 100%.

p5l7-ws2.note: Minutes 59 to 70.5. Children work alone on Q2 (printed on page 1) and Q4 (a) to (c); Q4 (d) and Q5 are take-home (starred). Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who add 20% and 25% in Q4. Page 2 has only two questions so that there is time to think. The percentage-change and deal questions are on the Think harder page (A1 and A2). Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q2 (a) to (d) (it is on page 1) and Q4 (a) to (c), then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 70.5 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l7-ws2ans.note: Minutes 70.5 to 73.5. One child explains Q2, the heaviest; click through the rest (Q4 (d) and Q5 are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click after a child explains. Q2a: 20% of $160 = $32, sale $128. Q2b: 10% of $128 = $12.80, 1% = $1.28, 9% = $11.52. Q2c: $128 + $11.52 = $139.52. Shop B is $140, so Shop A is 48¢ cheaper. Q4: 20% of $120 = $24; $96 left; 25% of $96 = $24; $72 left; $72 out of $120 = 60 out of 100. Ben forgot that 25% was of the remainder, not of $120. Q5: 10% of 40 = 4, so girls 60% = 24, boys 16; glasses 25% of 24 = 6, 50% of 16 = 8; 14 out of 40 = 35 out of 100. Think harder A1 (a puzzle that goes further): $1 out of the starting $4 is 25%; $1 out of the starting $5 is 20%. Think harder A2: X: pay for 3 boxes = $45. Y: 4 boxes = $60, 30% off = $18 off, $42. (b) one free box out of 4 = 25% off.

p5l7-teachchange.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use this after worksheet page 2, for children who go on to the Think harder page (A1), or at home. Percentage change goes beyond the page-1 and page-2 work, so say so: it is a puzzle that goes further, and the Percentage change = change out of the amount you START with line is all a child needs. Draw the two bars: $15 and $30. Click 1: the rise is $15, the starting price is $15, so $15 out of $15 is the whole thing again: 100% increase (doubling is a 100% increase, not 200%). Click 2: the fall is $15, but now the starting price is $30. $15 out of $30 is half: 50%. Say in words: "The percentage change is the change out of the STARTING amount." Ask: "Why are the two percentages not the same, when both changes are $15?" (the starting amount is different each time).

p5l7-teachdeal.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use this after worksheet page 2, for children who go on to the Think harder page (A2 compares two deals for 4 boxes). Ask first: "Which sounds better, a free pen or 30% off?" Let children vote, then work out both. Deal A: pay for 2 pens, $20. Deal B: $30 less 30% ($9) is $21. So the free pen wins here, by $1. Step 2: a free pen is $10 off $30, which is one third: about 33% off. On the worksheet the numbers are different and the answer is different: do not assume "buy and get free" always wins.

p5l7-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) (a) 25% ($1 out of $4) (b) 20% ($1 out of $5) (c) Each change is compared with its own starting amount: $1 out of $4 is a bigger part than $1 out of $5. (This is a puzzle that goes further than the lesson.) A2) (a) Shop X $45 (she pays for 3 boxes); Shop Y $42 (30% of $60 = $18 off). Shop Y is the better buy, by $3. (b) 25% off (1 box free out of 4, $15 off $60) A3) She found 10% ($8) and 5% (half of 10%, $4) and added them. 15% of $46 = $4.60 + $2.30 = $6.90. A4) Saved $30 (10% = $25, 2% = $5); sale price $220.

p5l7-stretch2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) (a) 25% ($1 out of $4) (b) 20% ($1 out of $5) (c) Each change is compared with its own starting amount: $1 out of $4 is a bigger part than $1 out of $5. (This is a puzzle that goes further than the lesson.) A2) (a) Shop X $45 (she pays for 3 boxes); Shop Y $42 (30% of $60 = $18 off). Shop Y is the better buy, by $3. (b) 25% off (1 box free out of 4, $15 off $60) A3) She found 10% ($8) and 5% (half of 10%, $4) and added them. 15% of $46 = $4.60 + $2.30 = $6.90. A4) Saved $30 (10% = $25, 2% = $5); sale price $220.

p5l7-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) No. $109 is 109% of the price before GST, so 1% is $1 and the GST is $9. (9% of $109 is wrong because GST is 9% of the price BEFORE GST.) B2) Shop P, by $1.20. P: $80 − $20 = $60. Q: $80 − $8 = $72, then 15% of $72 = $10.80 off, $61.20. B3) $120. Work backwards: $54 is 75% of the remainder, so the remainder is $72. $72 is 60% of her money, so 10% is $12 and 100% is $120. Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a price that goes up by a percentage and then down by the same percentage. Predict the final price, then test it. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l7-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q5 and Q7 (Q6, the two lamp shops, is only in the workbook). Answers: 1) No. $109 is 109% of the price before GST, so 1% = $1 and the price before GST was $100. The GST is $9, not $9.81. 2) $120. Work backwards: $54 is 75% of the money left after groceries, so that was $72; $72 is 60% of her money, so 10% is $12 and 100% is $120.

p5l7-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What is the whole in E1, and what is it 100% of? In B3, which amount is the new whole after the groceries? How many equal parts is $54? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l7-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. E1: the price tag already includes the GST, so $109 is 109% of the unknown price before GST. 109 ÷ 109 = 1: each 1% is $1, and the price before GST is $100, so the GST is $9. Ali took 9% of the wrong whole. B3: work backwards, undoing each step. After the gift, $54 is 75% of the money left, so a quarter of it is $18 and the money left was $72. After the groceries, 60% of her money is $72, so 10% is $12 and all of it is $120. Check forwards: 40% of $120 = $48 on groceries; $72 left; 25% of $72 = $18 gift; $54 left.

p5l7-talk.note: Minutes 73.5 to 79. Pairs try it with $100 for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: it is exactly the same. GST first: $109, then 20% off ($21.80) is $87.20. Discount first: $80, then 9% GST ($7.20) is $87.20. Each change is a multiplication, and the order of multiplying does not matter. Second question if time: Mei says "20% off and then 9% GST is the same as 11% off." Is she right? (No: 11% off $100 would be $89, but the real price is $87.20, because the GST is on the smaller sale price.) Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l7-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 84.5. Answer: $26.16. 20% of $30 = $6, sale price $24. 9% of $24: 10% = $2.40, 1% = $0.24, so 9% = $2.16. $24 + $2.16 = $26.16. Extension: a shop raises every price by 25%, then has a "20% off everything" sale. Is the sale price more than, less than or the same as the old price? Try $40, $100 and $64. (The same: up 25% then down 20% always gives back the old price. $40 to $50 to $40; $100 to $125 to $100; $64 to $80 to $64. Siti on the worksheet fell for the opposite trap: it is NOT the same as up 5%.)

p5l7-reflect.note: Minutes 84.5 to 87. REFLECTION, about a minute and a half. Children use the small box at the bottom of the Investigation and reflection page: Something I did well; The hardest part was; What helped me (tick boxes include "I asked for help" and "I am still stuck (my tutor will check in with me)"). Pass is always OK. Never collected in public; you may read it privately later to plan the next lesson and check in with any child who ticked still stuck in the open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, parent nearby, never a private message). Never read a child's reflection aloud. It is never collected or shown in public. You may read it privately afterwards to plan the next lesson and to check in with any child who ticked "I am still stuck", in the open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby, never a private message). Never read a child's reflection aloud; only a child who volunteers may share. Praise strategy, not speed: "Using 10% as a stepping stone got you unstuck." Then type the stamp in the chat for every child (one message) and say goodbye. If the clock is behind, the reflection becomes a one-tick version: pass or one box.
